The Centre for Research into Ecological and Environmental Modelling (CREEM) is hosting two linked workshops in the summer of 2016 at the University of St. Andrews, Scotland. This third announcement is to note

·         Earlybird registration discount will soon expire (see website URL at bottom of this note to reserve a place)

·         As part of the registration fee, participants will receive the 2015 book published by Springer Distance Sampling: Methods and Application by Buckland et al. that focuses upon topics of relevance to distance sampling practitioners.  The case studies found in this book will form the basis of both the introductory and advanced workshops.

The first workshop (16-19 August) will run at an introductory level, and will focus on distance sampling methods, largely described in the standard reference book "Introduction to Distance Sampling." The workshop will be a blend of theory and practice and participants will learn how to use the program "Distance." Participants will gain a solid grounding in both survey design and methods of analysis for distance sampling surveys.

The advanced distance sampling workshop (22-25 August) will include advanced treatment of analyses in which detectability on the transect line is not assumed to be perfect (the so-called g(0) problem) and spatial (or density surface) modelling. We will showcase a series of R packages for performing standard as well as sophisticated analyses in R.

For all workshops, participants are encouraged to bring their own data sets, and can expect to perform preliminary analyses of their data.  Participants can use our computers or bring their own laptops.

Additional details regarding the workshop contents and registration details can be found at our website
http://creem2.st-andrews.ac.uk/distance-sampling-workshops-st-andrews-august-2016-2/

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am conducting a CDS analysis using R on harbour porpoise line-transect data. My query relates to the calculated covered area which is very high compared to the total study area (A) and therefore looks wrong. As a result I am getting very low density, abundance and encounter rates. See figures below:

Summary for distance analysis

Number of observations :  55

Distance range         :  0  -  400

Model : Half-normal key function

AIC   : 640.3991

Detection function parameters

Scale Coefficients:

            estimate        se

(Intercept) 5.171927 0.1238487

                       Estimate          SE        CV

Average p             0.5394194  0.05737704 0.1063681

N in covered region 101.9614769 14.30675145 0.1403153

Summary for clusters

Summary statistics:

  Region   Area CoveredArea   Effort  n  k           ER        se.ER     cv.ER

1      1 136000   487871514 609839.4 55 48 9.018768e-05 1.636042e-05 0.1814042

Abundance:

  Label   Estimate          se        cv        lcl        ucl       df

1 Total 0.02842298 0.005977053 0.2102895 0.01878345 0.04300945 76.95691

Density:

  Label     Estimate           se        cv          lcl          ucl       df

1 Total 2.089925e-07 4.394892e-08 0.2102895 1.381136e-07 3.162459e-07 76.95691

Around half of the transects were surveyed twice but this still doesn’t explain the high covered area relative to total area. As I understand it the covered area should be 2wL (or is it 2wLPa?). If using the truncation value of 400m the calculation (2wL) seems almost correct at   487871520 m2 (but not quite, haven’t worked out how the figure presented was calculated). However, the Distance examples at www.distancesampling.org/R <http://www.distancesampling.org/R>  show outputs of covered area equal to survey area. Further to this, an estimate of 101 animals in a 136km2 area should surely not equate to such a low encounter rate and density value. Can you advise as to what has gone wrong here or if I am interpreting this incorrectly? The only thing I can think is wrong is the total length surveyed (L). I’ve looked over it and the length of each transect seems about right. Being on a vessel in strong currents, there is some variation in completed transect lengths compared to the pre-determined tracks and I have used the actual distance travelled. Perhaps this is a separate question, but would I be better to use the equal values of the pre-determined tracks?

Many thanks,

Gemma Veneruso

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Calculated covered area looks incorrect
messages.body_plain:
Gemma

It is useful that you have performed a "sense check" on your analysis, and have concluded that all is not as it should be.

My suspicion is that the units in which you measured your perpendicular distances (m possibly?) is not the same as the units in which you measured effort (transect length, km perhaps).  Unfortunately I don't know the units in which you measured either of those things.

Start from what you do know.  You should know the size of your study area (and the units in which it was measured); is 136000 correct?  Your email suggests the study area is 136km^2, so 136000 does not correspond to that either in km or in m.  The covered area of 487871514 divided by the effort (609839.4) *does* correspond to a truncation distance (w) of 400 (strip width=2w) as the output shows.

You can work back through your effort and perpendicular measurements and study area units to discern what has been entered improperly.  Read through the help regarding the argument "convert.units" in the function ds(); specifically the section of help entitled "Units" regarding that function.

messages.subject: Error message in MRDS engine "unexpected )" - an explanation and solution
messages.subject_clean: Error message in MRDS engine "unexpected )" - an explanation and solution
messages.body_plain:
Hi Folks,

A user recently reported to me getting an error message in the MRDS engine; we found the source of the problem so I thought I'd document it on the list in case anyone else gets the same issue.

Situation:
Using the MRDS engine to model double-platform data, wanting to fit an intercept-only MR model.  You get the following error message:
Error: unexpected ')' in "ddf.3<-ddf(method='io.fi <http://io.fi>',mrmodel=~glm(link='logit',formula=~)"
Execution halted

Solution:
Check whether you put
1
in the Model formula box under Model Definition Properties | Detection function | MR model.  If you left it blank you'll get the above error message.  Add 1 to the box and re-run, the error should disappear.

This is documented in the help, but it's rather obscure. In Chapter 10 - Mark Recapture Distance Sampling | Defining MRDS models | More About DS and MR Models it says:
"An intercept term is included in formulae by default.  To remove it you can use “- 1” - for example sex - 1, while to specify an intercept-only formula, you use 1 alone."

Best wishes to all, Len

Our department has collected data to estimate the abundance of three species of doves over 200 cities on an annual basis since 2008. So that said, for covariates for the detection function - we have City, Region, Species, Year, and Observer. Although I don't believe we will test observer effect due to some observer switching over the year - we would like to test both additive and interacting models with the other covariates. Currently, in Program Distance, I can truncate the dataset by city to do some of this - but I wanted to see if certain cities may have similar detection functions based on regional groupings or even some level of cover via remote sensing analysis. However, that doesn't get to the basis of doing model selection in comparing a wide variety of models. What would be the best path forward? These are single observer, cluster surveys where each point is conducted once annually.

Thank you.

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Understanding differences between detection functions
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris, list

I'll start by your second question, which is easier to address. You should not be worried about the fact that the "scale" of the histograms is different. The y-axis on the plot should be used only to read the detection probability as given by the fitted line, so by definition the line intercepts the y axis at one (since we assume g(0)=1 in conventional distance sampling). The histogram bars are simply rescaled such that the area above the line is the same as the area below the line. Something else that often raises questions (e.g. I have been explicitly asked by a reviewer about this, and it might look odd to folks not familiar with distance sampling data) is the fact that in your right plot one of the bars is above 1, yet a probability is bounded to be in the (0,1) interval. Again, this is not something to worry about, because the bars heights can't be interpreted on that y-axis scale.

Regarding your first question, sometimes a question just raises more questions ;) it is a bit difficult to know what might be going on without looking at the data, especially since you are using left truncation, which can be raise additional difficulties since to some extent one is asking the software to extrapolate a function to where there's no data. You do not really say much about sample size and the AIC values you are looking at. I know this is not your question, but why are you using left truncation? Is that due to the blind spot under the helicopter/airplane? I note that the HR model seems to fit worse in the tail, but in general it is not with the tail that you should be worried. I would say that the HN model seems to overshoot in an unexpected way, so might lead to an overestimation of density, and it being based on extrapolation of a fit in an area where you have no data, that might be questionable. As a side note, with not left truncated unbinned data often the opposite happens, with the HN model tending to average across spikes at small distances and the HR model leading to overestimation. How different are your density estimates from the two models? What are your sample sizes? Have you considered adjustment terms? Have you considered to just subtract 25 meters (or whatever distance you are left truncation the data at) to all the distances and fit a detection function to the data? I wonder if in such a case you will still get the HN model as the best fit, which if you do not might hint to problems with the current left truncation considered.

hope this helps, maybe others have additional comments re your first point

cheers

Tiago

Hi Tiago,

Thanks for the helpful comments on both questions.

You are right that I used left truncation because observers could not see directly below the aircraft. You were also right in your prediction that the density estimates from the HN model would be higher than that of the HR model.

models$hr.null.obs  <-  ds(distdata, key="hr", adjustment=NULL,  truncation=list(left=35.2,right=345.73),

Having a closer look at the parameter estimates, my naïve guess is that the HR model struggles to converge (although no warning is given) as the standard error of the “observer” parameter equals 203. If one compare this model to the HN model with observer as a covariate (SE = 0.108), the difference in AIC is 25 units.

The problem with ‘observer’ ''disappears'' if I add ‘size’ (cluster size) to the HR model as an additional covariate (observer SE = 0.08, size SE = 0.07). This model is then also better ranked than the corresponding HN model with additive observer and size effects(~ 5 units).

The sample size is 662 observations. I have not looked what happens to the HR model with observer if the truncation distance is subtracted from all the distances, but this new detection function appears to work fine.

Thanks again!
Chris

messages.body_plain:
Shaun

Trying to get my head around your interests. Are you trying to produce year-city specific density estimates for each species?  Or year-region-species estimates?

At face value, if you treat 'city' as a factor covariate and the only covariate in your model, your detection function model will have 200+ parameters.  I would expect trouble when trying to fit such a beast.  Not to mention what might happen when other covariates such as year are included as well.  A mission to tackle detection function models with main effects and interactions would indeed by a monumental undertaking, with what I would predict, could be challenges in convergence with such large parameter spaces.

You might stand a better chance of success with your 'region' approach, whereby the number of levels of the covariate associated with geography is <10 (say 4 or 5). Even then, you may have 4 levels of 'region', 8 levels of 'year' and 3 levels of 'species', a main effects only model would have 96ish parameters.  Taking the route of a remote sensing covariate could convert your factor covariate region to a continuous covariate and knock down your full model to a more reasonable 25ish parameters.

Dear Eric and mailing list,

A very belated thank you for your last reply Eric. It turns out that I had simply converted my area units incorrectly resulting in too small a density!

I have a separate query now. It has been mentioned to me that spatial autocorrelation could be an issue if not analysed appropriately. To remind you of my dataset, I have conducted around 12 months of (almost monthly) line-transect survey data at sea with a view of estimating harbour porpoise density. I designed a series of zig zag transect lines equally spaced from one another, each of which were chosen at random per survey. Each leg within a single transect was treated as an independent sample. Some lines have been surveyed more than once (months apart from each other). Between one and two transects were surveyed per day.

It has been suggested that spatial autocorrelation could be present and should be accounted for, perhaps because I have classified a sample as a survey leg. I’m struggling to get my head around this concept…If you have locations A, B and C in increasing distance from one another. Detection 1 is at A. If spatially correlated, detection 2 is most likely to occur at B compared to C due to the closer vicinity of A. Is this spatial autocorrelation??

If I look at a GIS plots of my data and think back to surveys, there are certain days were a lot more animals are seen in a short space of time (and space) than others. However, in reality most marine mammal datasets should see this since there will be some feature (spatial or temporal) that is attractive to an animal, and therefore other animals….I do not think that I see a trend of many detections on one leg resulting in a glut of detections on the next leg. Is this what I need to check? For info. each leg is around 5 km and takes about 30 mins to complete. There are certainly no concentrations of detections at the start and end of legs where the distance between these is the smallest. It is true that the encounter rate is highly variable depending on the day. However this has been balanced out temporally by ensuring almost even coverage of the temporal feature that I believe may drive porpoise distribution. But now I’m talking about temporal autocorrelation….I think…I’m confused!

Lastly Buckland et al 2001 p 130 states that the assumption of objects being detected and distributed independently is not a significant issue when estimating density.

If anyone could help relieve my confusion and advise on whether I have an issue here that would be much appreciated!

Many thanks again for your time,

Gemma

Gemma

It is useful that you have performed a "sense check" on your analysis, and have concluded that all is not as it should be.

My suspicion is that the units in which you measured your perpendicular distances (m possibly?) is not the same as the units in which you measured effort (transect length, km perhaps).  Unfortunately I don't know the units in which you measured either of those things.

Start from what you do know.  You should know the size of your study area (and the units in which it was measured); is 136000 correct?  Your email suggests the study area is 136km^2, so 136000 does not correspond to that either in km or in m.  The covered area of 487871514 divided by the effort (609839.4) *does* correspond to a truncation distance (w) of 400 (strip width=2w) as the output shows.

You can work back through your effort and perpendicular measurements and study area units to discern what has been entered improperly.  Read through the help regarding the argument "convert.units" in the function ds(); specifically the section of help entitled "Units" regarding that function.

messages.body_plain:
Hello again,

I’m writing an update to my previous email found below regarding spatial autocorrelation. I’ve got my head round this now and will conduct a couple of tests to see if it is significant for my dataset. But my question is; does it actually matter if spatial autocorrelation exists when simply providing an overall density estimate of a survey area if there is no temporal autocorrelation? I can’t think why this would be an issue unless you are interested in splitting the area into blocks, investigating distribution or incorporating this estimate into certain types of model to predict a cause of impact for example. Please correct me if I am wrong!?

Many thanks again,

Gemma Veneruso

Dear Eric and mailing list,

A very belated thank you for your last reply Eric. It turns out that I had simply converted my area units incorrectly resulting in too small a density!

I have a separate query now. It has been mentioned to me that spatial autocorrelation could be an issue if not analysed appropriately. To remind you of my dataset, I have conducted around 12 months of (almost monthly) line-transect survey data at sea with a view of estimating harbour porpoise density. I designed a series of zig zag transect lines equally spaced from one another, each of which were chosen at random per survey. Each leg within a single transect was treated as an independent sample. Some lines have been surveyed more than once (months apart from each other). Between one and two transects were surveyed per day.

It has been suggested that spatial autocorrelation could be present and should be accounted for, perhaps because I have classified a sample as a survey leg. I’m struggling to get my head around this concept…If you have locations A, B and C in increasing distance from one another. Detection 1 is at A. If spatially correlated, detection 2 is most likely to occur at B compared to C due to the closer vicinity of A. Is this spatial autocorrelation??

If I look at a GIS plots of my data and think back to surveys, there are certain days were a lot more animals are seen in a short space of time (and space) than others. However, in reality most marine mammal datasets should see this since there will be some feature (spatial or temporal) that is attractive to an animal, and therefore other animals….I do not think that I see a trend of many detections on one leg resulting in a glut of detections on the next leg. Is this what I need to check? For info. each leg is around 5 km and takes about 30 mins to complete. There are certainly no concentrations of detections at the start and end of legs where the distance between these is the smallest. It is true that the encounter rate is highly variable depending on the day. However this has been balanced out temporally by ensuring almost even coverage of the temporal feature that I believe may drive porpoise distribution. But now I’m talking about temporal autocorrelation….I think…I’m confused!

Lastly Buckland et al 2001 p 130 states that the assumption of objects being detected and distributed independently is not a significant issue when estimating density.

If anyone could help relieve my confusion and advise on whether I have an issue here that would be much appreciated!

Many thanks again for your time,

Gemma

Gemma

It is useful that you have performed a "sense check" on your analysis, and have concluded that all is not as it should be.

My suspicion is that the units in which you measured your perpendicular distances (m possibly?) is not the same as the units in which you measured effort (transect length, km perhaps).  Unfortunately I don't know the units in which you measured either of those things.

Start from what you do know.  You should know the size of your study area (and the units in which it was measured); is 136000 correct?  Your email suggests the study area is 136km^2, so 136000 does not correspond to that either in km or in m.  The covered area of 487871514 divided by the effort (609839.4) *does* correspond to a truncation distance (w) of 400 (strip width=2w) as the output shows.

You can work back through your effort and perpendicular measurements and study area units to discern what has been entered improperly.  Read through the help regarding the argument "convert.units" in the function ds(); specifically the section of help entitled "Units" regarding that function.
